args.text: --- title: 'Hello World' description: 'Change the FHE computation in the default template so that the E3 returns two times the sum, and run it again.' --- import { Callout, Steps } from 'nextra/components' import { Flow, LinkCard, LinkCards } from '@/components/ui' # Hello World This tutorial has a fiddle with the FHE computation in the default template and gives the E3 another run. It's for developers who've already knocked over the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start). By the end, your E3 hands back 2 × (a + b) instead of a + b, and you'll know which files hold the computation, its test, and its labels in the client. ## Before you begin You'll need the `my-first-e3` project from the [Quick Start](/build/quick-start), untouched. Every path on this page is relative to the project folder. ## How the template computes The FHE computation is the one Rust function, `fhe_processor`, in `program/src/lib.rs`. The rest of the template just ferries ciphertexts to this function and carts its result off to the committee. 1. The client encrypts each number with the committee public key and calls `MyProgram.publishInput`. 2. Once the input window shuts, the coordination server (`server/index.ts`) reads the published inputs and sends them over to the program server on port 13151. 3. The program server (`.interfold/support/dev/src/main.rs`) calls `fhe_processor` and sends the encrypted result back to the coordination server. 4. The coordination server publishes the encrypted result, and the committee decrypts it. Here's the default computation in `program/src/lib.rs`, with the doc comment above `policy` taken out: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" use e3_compute_provider::{FHEProcessorInput, InputPolicy}; use fhe::bfv::Ciphertext; use fhe_traits::{DeserializeParametrized, Serialize}; pub fn policy() -> InputPolicy { InputPolicy::default() } /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } sum.to_bytes() } ``` - `FHEProcessorInput` has two fields. `ciphertexts` yields `(Vec, u64)` pairs one at a time: the serialized ciphertext and its input index. `params` holds the BFV parameters of the E3. - `Ciphertext::zero` makes the zero ciphertext, the starting value. The `+=` operator adds each input ciphertext onto it. This addition is homomorphic: the function adds up the hidden values, but it can't get a look at them. - `sum.to_bytes()` serializes the encrypted result. - `policy()` returns the input policy. The default policy uses every published input, the lot. The template requests E3s with the `insecure-512` parameter set. Its plaintext modulus is 100, so every result gets worked out modulo 100. For this tutorial, 2 × (a + b) has to come in under 100. ## Change the computation ### Stop the stack If `pnpm dev:all` is running, hit `Ctrl+C` in its terminal. ### Double the encrypted sum In `program/src/lib.rs`, swap the `fhe_processor` function out for this version: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" {9-11} /// Implementation of the CiphertextProcessor function pub fn fhe_processor(fhe_inputs: FHEProcessorInput<'_>) -> Vec { let mut sum = Ciphertext::zero(fhe_inputs.params); for (bytes, _) in fhe_inputs.ciphertexts { let ciphertext = Ciphertext::from_bytes(&bytes, fhe_inputs.params).unwrap(); sum += &ciphertext; } // Add the encrypted sum to itself. The hidden value becomes 2 × (a + b). let doubled = &sum + ∑ doubled.to_bytes() } ``` `&sum + &sum` adds two ciphertexts and returns a new ciphertext. The function doesn't need any new imports. ### Update the unit test The test down the bottom of `program/src/lib.rs` encrypts 3 and 2 and calls `fhe_processor`. Change the expected value from 5 to 10: ```rust filename="program/src/lib.rs" let tally = Vec::::try_decode(&decrypted, Encoding::poly())?; assert_eq!(tally[0], 10); Ok(()) ``` ### Run the unit test ```bash cargo test -p e3-user-program ``` Cargo prints `test tests::test ... ok`. If the test falls over, check your `fhe_processor` against the code in the step before. ### Update the label on the input step In `client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx`, track down this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: {input1} + {input2} = ? ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/EnterInputs.tsx" Ready to compute: 2 × ({input1} + {input2}) = ? ``` ### Update the label on the results step Over in `client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx`, find this line: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2} = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` Change it to: ```tsx filename="client/src/pages/steps/Results.tsx" { submittedInputs ? `2 × (${submittedInputs.input1} + ${submittedInputs.input2}) = ${result !== null ? result : '…'}` : '…' } ``` ### Start the stack ```bash pnpm dev:all ``` The `PROGRAM` process runs `interfold program start`. In dev mode, that command runs `cargo run --bin e3-support-scripts-dev`, so Cargo compiles the program server again with your new `fhe_processor` baked in. ### Run an E3 Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000). If the client's still showing the result of an earlier E3, select **Start over** in the top bar. Request an E3, then punch in 5 and 3. The input step shows `Ready to compute: 2 × (5 + 3) = ?`. The results step shows `2 × (5 + 3) = 16`. Too easy. ## Why nothing else changes - **The contract.** `MyProgram.publishInput` stores a commitment for each input, and `MyProgram.verify` checks the compute proof. Neither function has the computation in it. - **The coordination server.** `server/index.ts` sends every published input to the program server and publishes whatever output it gets back. It's got no idea what the computation does. - **The deployment.** `pnpm dev:all` deploys the contracts again on a fresh local chain every time it starts. In dev mode, the program server runs `fhe_processor` without a proof, and the template deploys `MockOpenVmReceiptVerifier`, which waves through every receipt on the local chain. With real proofs, `MyProgram.verify` checks the OpenVM receipt against the `imageId` that `MyProgram` gets handed when it's deployed. Change the program and that identity changes too, so compile and deploy again. See [Compute provider](/build/e3-program/compute-provider). ## Update the integration test The template's got an end-to-end test in `tests/integration.spec.ts`. It encrypts 1 and 2 and expects their sum. Now that you've made your change, update the expected value: ```ts filename="tests/integration.spec.ts" expect(BigInt(result)).toBe(2n * (num1 + num2)) ``` Run the test with `pnpm test:integration`. This test needs a CLI built with the `test-only-skip-proof-aggregation` Cargo feature, and the release binaries don't come with it. See [Installation](/build/installation#install-the-cli) for a source build. ## Operations on ciphertexts The template uses the `fhe` crate from `gnosisguild/fhe.rs` at tag `v0.4.2`. For a `Ciphertext`, that crate implements these operators: | Operation | Operator | Example | | --------------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------- | | Add two ciphertexts | `+`, `+=` | `&a + &b` | | Subtract two ciphertexts | `-`, `-=` | `&a - &b` | | Negate a ciphertext | unary `-` | `-&a` | | Add or subtract a plaintext | `+`, `+=`, `-`, `-=` | `&a + &plaintext` | | Multiply by a plaintext | `*`, `*=` | `&a * &plaintext` | A `Plaintext` has to use the same parameters object as the ciphertext, that is, `fhe_inputs.params`. If the parameters objects don't match, the operator panics. Every result wraps modulo the plaintext modulus. A negative result, say from `&a - &b` with `a < b`, wraps round to a big value. The crate also implements `*` for two ciphertexts, but the default template doesn't use it and this page doesn't go into it. ## Next steps Write the FHE computation for your very own E3 program. Validate inputs and verify proofs in your E3 program contract. Track down the file to edit for each bit of the template.
